items.title: Groeien in je rol als vrijwilligerscoördinator, hoe doe je dat?
items.raw_text: Voor iedere beroepskracht werken er bij openbare bibliotheken gemiddeld ruim drie vrijwilligers. Samen houden zij de bibliotheek draaiend. Goede samenwerking en begeleiding zijn dus belangrijk; onderwerpen waar vrijwilligerscoördinatoren volop mee bezig zijn. Hun rol verandert. Van zelf alles regelen en oplossen naar verbinden, signaleren en overzicht houden. Maar hoe maak je die stap in de praktijk? En wat vraagt dat van de vrijwilligerscoördinator? Saskia Dik, vrijwilligerscoördinator bij Bibliotheek West-Achterhoek, ontdekte het tijdens een coachingstraject met organisatieadviseur Annemiek Messer. Het leverde haar niet alleen nieuwe inzichten op, maar ook meer vertrouwen in haar rol. Zoals ze zelf zegt: ‘Ik ben de goede persoon op de goede plek’. Ontdek welke lessen Annemiek meegaf aan Saskia en laat je inspireren. Saskia Dik met vrijwilliger Jos Hesseling De juiste persoon Saskia werkt ruim 12,5 jaar bij Bibliotheek West-Achterhoek. Eerst als roosteraar, inmiddels als vrijwilligerscoördinator. Ruim drie jaar geleden kwam die vacature vrij en daar had Saskia wel oren naar, vertelt ze. ‘Ik bedacht: wil ik hier de laatste jaren tot mijn pensioen de roosters blijven maken? items.title: Prinsjesdag 2026: 5 thema’s uitgelicht voor bibliotheken
items.raw_text: Prinsjesdag 2026 zit erop. De nieuw gepresenteerde plannen laten zien dat het kabinet vertrouwen heeft in de toekomst van bibliotheken. Er komt meer zekerheid voor leesbevordering, bibliotheken krijgen een belangrijke maatschappelijke rol en er is geld voor verdere ontwikkeling. Tegelijkertijd zijn er ook uitdagingen. Gaby Erckens, onze teamleider Financiën en Control, dook in de plannen en zette de belangrijkste 5 thema’s op een rij. 1. Structureel geld voor leesbevordering Goed nieuws is dat de programma’s BoekStart en de Bibliotheek op school vanaf 2027 structurele financiering krijgen. Dat betekent dat je als bibliotheek of school niet langer afhankelijk bent van tijdelijke subsidies. Voor 2027 is hiervoor €38 miljoen beschikbaar. Vanaf 2028 groeit dit naar €50 miljoen per jaar. Bibliotheken en scholen kunnen dus langdurige plannen maken en blijven investeren in leesplezier, taalontwikkeling en onderwijs. 2. Iedereen heeft toegang tot een bibliotheek Het kabinet zet een belangrijke stap richting een wettelijke zorgplicht voor bibliotheken. Het doel: voor iedereen een bibliotheek in de buurt. Om gemeenten hierbij te ondersteunen, stelt het Rijk jaarlijks ongeveer € 60 miljoen beschikbaar. Ook kleinere gemeenten krijgen ondersteuning. Voor hen geldt een minimumbedrag van €100.000, zodat lokale bibliotheekvoorzieningen behouden blijven of opnieuw kunnen openen. Wat deze ontwikkeling laat zien? items.title: Lezen dichter bij studenten: de kracht van samenwerken
items.raw_text: Zeven schoolbibliotheken op zeven locaties. Dat is het doel van de samenwerking tussen ROC van Twente, vier Overijsselse bibliotheken en Rijnbrink. Op maandag 7 september werd de eerste Bibliotheek op school officieel geopend bij ROC-locatie Wierdensestraat in Almelo. Een mooi voorbeeld van hoe bovenlokale samenwerking lezen dichter bij studenten kan brengen. En van hoe we ze samen veel meer bijbrengen dan een vak. Erwin Karst was als adviseur bij Rijnbrink aanjager van deze bovenlokale samenwerking. Een proces van meerdere jaren, met veel gesprekken, voorlichtingen en workshops om opleidingen en docenten mee te krijgen. Hij zag de afgelopen jaren een duidelijke verandering in het middelbaar beroepsonderwijs. ‘Er is een toenemend besef van urgentie dat ook mbo-scholen iets met lezen moeten doen. Waar ik eerder vaak in een soort overtuigingsstand de scholen langs ging, zijn veel scholen het er inmiddels over eens hoe belangrijk leesbevordering voor studenten is. Een goed teken, ook gezien recent onderzoek waaruit blijkt dat de leesvaardigheid onder Nederlandse scholieren verder daalt . items.title: Vacature directeur / bestuurder
items.raw_text: Wil jij richting geven aan een organisatie die overheid, bedrijfsleven, kenniswereld en maatschappij bij elkaar brengt op het gebied van digitalisering? Kun jij maatschappelijke en bestuurlijke vraagstukken verbinden aan concrete samenwerking én zorgen voor een professionele en toekomstbestendige organisatie? Dan is dit jouw kans om betekenisvolle impact te maken. Binnen Stichting ECP | Platform voor de InformatieSamenleving is namelijk de vacature ontstaan voor een: directeur-bestuurder Wat ga je doen? ECP heeft al ruim 25 jaar een bewezen meerwaarde door haar verbindende kracht, neutrale opstelling en breed gedragen en geïmplementeerde resultaten van programma’s en projecten. ECP bevindt zich op dit moment in een belangrijke fase in haar ontwikkeling: in de periode 2026–2028 werkt ECP aan een transitie gericht op het borgen van continuïteit, het professionaliseren van de governance en het toekomstbestendig maken van de organisatie, met behoud van de kernwaarden. De Directeur-Bestuurder fungeert als boegbeeld en stuurt op deze transitie. Daarbij geldt dat je niet primair technisch verantwoordelijk bent voor dagelijkse procesuitvoering, maar wel borgt dat ECP intern voldoende in samenhang is georganiseerd, zodat governance, kwaliteit en financiële beheersing op orde zijn. items.title: Nederlanders denken dat ze phishing herkennen, maar AI maakt oplichting steeds echter en juist dát is een groot veiligheidsrisico
items.raw_text: Uit het jaarlijkse nationale cybersecurityonderzoek van Alert Online, mede mogelijk gemaakt door het ministerie van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, blijkt dat Nederlanders wél weten wat veilig online gedrag is, maar gemiddeld slechts een derde van de veilige handelingen consequent toepassen. Den Haag – Nederlanders weten goed hoe ze zich online moeten beschermen, maar vertrouwen opvallend vaak op hun eigen vermogen om gevaar te herkennen. Zodra er meer van hen gevraagd wordt dan kijken, neemt de motivatie om zich veilig te gedragen af. Slechts één op de zes gebruikt altijd tweefactorauthenticatie, een dubbel slot voor je accounts en apparaten dat ervoor zorgt dat er meer nodig is dan een wachtwoord om in te loggen. Zo kunnen criminelen met een gestolen wachtwoord niet zomaar een account overnemen. En maar drie op de tien gaan altijd zelf naar de officiële website in plaats van op een link te klikken. Dat blijkt uit het nationale cybersecurityonderzoek van Alert Online, dat vandaag verschijnt bij de start van de Europese cybersecuritymaand. Wie denkt zelf phishing te herkennen, slaat in veel gevallen de stappen over die je écht beschermen. Ook weten mensen vaak niet hóé ze iets instellen, zien ze anderen het niet doen en voelt het als te veel werk. AI maakt oplichting overtuigender en bedrijfsdata kwetsbaarder Met het toegenomen AI-gebruik groeien de risico’s. items.title: Podcastaflevering over Digitaal Doordacht en de praktijkimpact van digitalisering
items.raw_text: ECP-directeur Arie van Bellen ging in een recente aflevering van de podcastreeks ECP Talks in gesprek met ECP-programmaregisseur Sabine Herbrink over het programma Digitaal Doordacht. Zij bespraken hoe het programma de overheid helpt om bewuste, doordachte keuzes te maken in onze snel digitaliserende samenleving. Het gesprek ging niet alleen over de kansen zoals dwarsverbanden tussen thema’s en de meerwaarde die het programma biedt in de digitalisering van de overheid, maar ook over de uitdagingen rondom verantwoorde inzet, innovatie en samenwerking. Meer weten? Beluister de aflevering ‘Praktijkimpact van digitalisering’ Het bericht Podcastaflevering over Digitaal Doordacht en de praktijkimpact van digitalisering verscheen eerst op ECP | Platform voor de InformatieSamenleving .

items.title: Van regisserende naar ontwerpende overheid
items.raw_text: Van AI-experiment naar digitaal opdrachtgeverschap Veranderverhalen vanuit ECP | Platform voor de Informatiesamenleving ECP | Platform voor de Informatiesamenleving brengt met een reeks veranderverhalen in beeld hoe professionals binnen de overheid werken aan betekenisvolle digitalisering. In de gesprekken met Marc Minnee en Marco de Bruijn van het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) staat centraal waar verandering daadwerkelijk ontstaat: wanneer professionals elkaar vinden, aannames bespreekbaar maken en keuzes maken die bijdragen aan versnelling én duurzame borging. Zo laten de verhalen zien hoe digitalisering door concrete interventies kan bijdragen aan een toekomstgerichte overheid waarin burgers en ondernemers centraal staan, met blijvende aandacht voor ethiek, privacy, security en maatschappelijk vertrouwen. Op 24 juni vond in Amare voor de vijfde keer de CIO-dag plaats. Voor een zaal vol CIO’s schetsten Marc Minnee, innovatiemanager voor het ministerie van BZK, en Marco de Bruijn, beleidsmedewerker AI bij het ministerie van BZK, hun NDS AI-visie op de inzet van generatieve AI-modellen bij de overheid. Hun verhaal begint bij taalmodellen, maar raakt al snel aan een veel fundamentelere vraag: hoe houdt de overheid zelf regie over haar digitale toekomst? Binnen de Nederlandse Digitaliseringsstrategie is AI daarom een prioriteit: de overheid wil AI verantwoord inzetten voor maatschappelijke opgaven en betere dienstverlening, succesvolle toepassin

items.title: OTC Whitepaper Soevereiniteit
items.raw_text: Digitale soevereiniteit betekent niet dat organisaties alle digitale diensten zelf moeten bezitten of beheren. Het betekent dat zij aantoonbare grip hebben op kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden: inzicht in de keten, bewuste risicoacceptatie, uitvoerbare alternatieven, onafhankelijke controle en transparante communicatie over keuzes en restrisico’s. In het whitepaper over digitale soevereiniteit vertaalt de Online Trust Coalitie dit thema naar een praktisch handelingskader voor bestuurders, IT-verantwoordelijken, toezichthouders, serviceproviders en risk- en compliancefuncties. De OTC stelt dat digitale soevereiniteit niet draait om volledige autonomie of autarkie, maar om aantoonbare beheersing: inzicht in kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden, expliciete risicoafweging, uitvoerbare exit-mogelijkheden, onafhankelijke controle en heldere communicatie over restrisico’s en gemaakte keuzes. De OTC signaleert dat impliciet vertrouwen in digitale diensten onder druk staat. items.title: When Books Become a Bridge: The UAF Bibliotherapy Corner
items.raw_text: University students regularly struggle with academic pressure, social isolation, financial stress, and excessive screen time. Recognizing these challenges, the University of Agriculture, Faisalabad (UAF), under the visionary leadership of its Vice Chancellor, launched Pakistan’s first formal Bibliotherapy Corner in its Main Library. The initiative shows how innovation can achieve significant impact with zero budget. By bringing together four existing resources—library space, selected books, library staff, and volunteer psychologists—the UAF Library created a welcoming environment and a safe space where students receive both emotional support and guided reading. In partnership with Health 360, volunteer psychologists conduct counseling sessions, while library staff have indexed relevant books by themes such as exam anxiety, homesickness, self-confidence, and stress management, enabling students to quickly access the most helpful pages in the books. The University of Agriculture, Faisalabad UAF launched Pakistan s first formal Bibliotherapy Corner in its Main Library The outcome is promising. Within a short period, 76 students received free counseling and bibliotherapy support. Around 90% of the participants were female students, highlighting the importance of providing a safe, approachable, and stigma-free space for students seeking help. items.title: Your voice matters! Report from the FAIFE/MLAS Banned Books Week webinar
items.raw_text: During Banned Books Week 2026 FAIFE and MLAS hosted the webinar Let Books Be: A Global Conversation on the Freedom to Read , with special focus on the freedom to read in public and school libraries. Three speakers highlighted important issues from their fields of work: Giuseppe Meliti, from the Italian Library Association Observatory on Censorship , Corinthia Price, president of the International Association of School Librarianship , and Laura Winton, CEO of St. Albert Public Library , Alberta, and former Vice-Chair of the Canadian Federation of Library Associations . In this news item, we provide a short summary of their presentations. Silent increase of challenges and normalisation of insecurity as a working condition Giuseppe Meliti talked about the results of a survey that the observatory had sent out to Italian libraries in 2025. Mostly public libraries had responded to the survey and over half of the respondents had reported that safeguards against censorship in libraries were inadequate. The survey demonstrated a normalisation of insecurity as a working condition, and self-censorship was perceived as an increased risk for libraries, although among respondents the awareness of self-censorship risks was high (~73 %). Another insight from the survey was that there had been 110 reported cases of censorship or attempts of censorship in libraries from respondents, an increase from 40 cases in 2022, indicating a silent increase in the number of challenges. items.title: Call for Proposals: Artificial Intelligence in Collection Development and Acquisitions
items.raw_text: IFLA Acquisitions and Collection Development Section — Webinar, February 2027 The Acquisitions and Collection Development Section (ACD) of IFLA invites proposals for a webinar on the use of artificial intelligence in collection development and acquisitions, to be held in February 2027. AI tools are beginning to change how libraries build and manage their collections. Librarians are using them to analyze usage patterns, anticipate demand, and make the routine work of acquisitions and collection management faster and more responsive to what users need. This webinar is mostly about those opportunities. We also want to consider the risks, from selection bias to recommendations for outdated or nonexistent material to the environmental cost of large language models and open questions about author rights. We are sure that creative work is being done in this area and are looking forward to hearing from the librarians doing it. We are looking for case studies from libraries of different sizes, types, and regions. We are less interested in speculation about what AI might someday do than in accounts of what libraries are actually doing now: what has worked, what has not, and what others should know before trying something similar. Our focus is on AI as a tool for doing the work of collection development and acquisitions: informing selection and deselection, analyzing use, and improving acquisitions workflows. items.title: Quiet Powerhouses: Leadership Lessons from an Academic Library in a Nigerian University of Technology

Introduction I often say that working in a university library in Nigeria isn’t for the faint-hearted, but leading one at a university of technology? That’s a calling all on its own. As the University Librarian at Ladoke Akintola University of Technology (LAUTECH), I operate in a space where passion, pressure, and purpose intersect. It’s a role that requires resilience, vision, and unwavering belief in the transformative power of information services, especially within an institution rooted in science and technology, situated in a region where infrastructure and funding can be unpredictable. items.title: Metropolitan Libraries Spotlight: How Nanhai Library Is Reconnecting Children with the Classics
items.raw_text: When a thousand-year-old novel has to compete with a 15-second video In Foshan, in the heart of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, Nanhai Library serves a district of more than 3.7 million people, where local families, migrant workers, students, and seniors intertwine in a fast-moving, diverse community. It is also a community facing a very contemporary problem: as short-form video quietly absorbs every spare moment of screen time, deep reading is being pushed to the margins, even when the content at stake is centuries old. Rather than treat this as a lost cause, the library decided to meet children where their attention already lives. In April 2026, it launched Classics 101: Mental Models for Kids, a program built specifically for 10- to 12-year-olds — the exact age when children move from picture-to-text bridge books into more demanding reading. Making the classics legible again The challenge was concrete and specific. More than 60% of students in the first sessions admitted their biggest frustration was simple: they could not remember who everyone was or how all the characters connected. The semi-archaic language, sprawling character webs, and unhurried pacing of China’s Four Great Classical Novels were never designed to compete with instant gratification. So Nanhai Library stopped asking children to memorize plots and started extracting something more useful: practical mental models drawn directly from the characters’ journeys. items.title: Learning by Doing: IFLA Futures Club #5
items.raw_text: The fifth edition of the IFLA Futures Club offered an opportunity to explore what it looks like to apply futures thinking in libraries, in reality. Erik Boekesteijn and Cathelijne Kuiters of the Dutch National Library (KB) joined us to talk about their experience of running a concerted initiative to make futures thinking a more central part of the institution’s work, both with a view to shaping a new policy plan, and building skills more broadly. This was not the first time that futures had been on the agenda at the KB. Already, a ‘Club Stof’ had brought together colleagues throughout the sector, keen to get to grips with ‘the uncomfortable uncertainty of the future’. But with awareness that we are in a time where pre-existing ideas and assumptions are being challenged – epistemic turbulence – the Library’s new leadership was ready to take this work up a gear. There was an awareness from the start that this work provided an opportunity to think more broadly. First of all, an initaitive like this in the KB is not just an internal exercise, but also has potential impacts across the wider library field. National libraries usually have a kind of leadership within their fields, but the Dutch one has a formal role in supporting the country’s network of national libraries. What it does has the possibility to feed into changes across every local authority in the country. items.title: Authors Discuss Being Banned, Part 2: Malinda Lo, Ellen Hopkins, and Jennifer L. Armentrout
items.raw_text: The troubling trend of book challenges and bans in libraries across the US continues. In 2025, 4,235 titles were banned or challenged at public, school, or university libraries, according to the American Library Association’s (ALA) State of America’s Libraries 2026 report. This figure was the second highest (following the record set in 2023) since ALA’s Office for Intellectual Freedom (OIF) began documenting censorship attempts in 1990. Behind each title is an author being professionally—and sometimes personally—targeted for the stories they have chosen to share. These works usually amplify marginalized voices such as abuse victims or those within the LGBTQ+ community. American Libraries spoke with five authors on the Top 11 Most Challenged Books of 2025 list included in the report to hear how their experiences affected them. Interviews have been edited for space and clarity. Read Part 1 for the first two interviews with Patricia McCormick and Stephen Chbosky. Set in 1950s San Francisco, the book tells the story of 17-year-old Lily Hu as she navigates falling in love in a place and time not ready to accept a same-sex couple. items.raw_text: Library renovations can feel overwhelming—especially when you’re juggling tight budgets, big community expectations, and a building that’s showing its age. The good news is you don’t have to choose between “do nothing” and “tear it down.” Most successful library upgrades live somewhere in the middle: a smart, phased plan that protects your long-term vision while making meaningful improvements right now. Here are a few practical ways to think about approaching a library renovation: Start with a North Star. Before you pick finishes or start talking timelines, take a step back and get clarity on what you want your library to become. I call this the north star —your vision for how the building should function for staff and the public. Even if you only have funding for part of the work today, guiding principles help you avoid spending money on changes you’ll undo later. Renovations are much easier when everyone can point to the same end goal—even if you’re getting there in phases. Assess the building first. It’s tempting to jump straight into visible improvements, but understanding existing conditions is what sets a project up for success. A solid facility-condition evaluation looks at the status of major building systems and flags components that may be nearing the end of their life cycle, such as mechanical systems, electrical panel capacity, and even finishes like carpet. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . items.title: Report: Minnesota Banned Book Bans, So Why Are Books Still Being Pulled From Shelves?
items.raw_text: From The Star Tribune: Two Minnesota schools have been among the national leaders in library book bans the past two years, despite a law here that first banned book bans in 2024. So, if it’s illegal, how did these books get pulled from shelves? The law lacks teeth, legal experts say, because it doesn’t lay out enforcement details or potential penalties. The law prohibits public libraries from banning books based on their messages and ideas. But it lacks enforcement, said Jane Kirtley, professor emerita of media ethics and law at the University of Minnesota. “The trouble with any kind of law dealing with restrictions on speech is that it’s not self-executing,” she said. It exists and people are supposed to follow it, but with no stated consequences or enforcement means, it can be violated without punishment, Kirtley said. [Clip] A growing number of states has enacted laws against book bans, said Sarah Lamdan, executive director of the American Library Association’s Office for Intellectual Freedom. Such laws protect readers’ rights and library workers, she said. About a dozen states have them, with several more considering their own ban ban. Some states have enforcement mechanisms or do things like limit funding when a law is broken, she said. And while some state laws may lack teeth, they still indicate that a state opposes book banning, said Lynn Oberlander, a partner with the law firm Ballard Spahr. items.title: OpenAlex Announces Launch of Trusted Journal Lists
items.raw_text: From an OpenAlex Post: Trust in science is under more pressure than it has been in a long time. Paper mills, hijacked journals, citation rings and a flood of machine-written manuscripts mean that “is this a real journal?” is now a question every reader, reviewer, funder and university has to ask. And the tools for answering it have not kept up. The traditional answer is a deny list. Something like the old Beall’s List : a roster of predatory journals, so you can filter them out of a search, an evaluation, a systematic review. We understand the appeal. Nobody wants to cite a paper mill by accident. But we’re not building a deny list, and we don’t think you want one either. Librarians have been making this case for a decade : deny lists are opaque , they go stale the moment they’re published, they’re a lawsuit magnet , and they land hardest on exactly the journals that can least absorb the hit… small, new, non-English, Global South. Beall’s List went dark in 2017 . The advice since then has been consistent: don’t filter out the bad, filter in the good. Use allow lists . [Clip] In the era of the legacy indexes, “approved” meant one thing: is it in the index? That made a kind of sense when a couple of companies ran the only lists. It makes less sense now, because different questions need different lists. We launched in September with twenty-two, and we keep adding more: there are 61 now . items.raw_text: From ZBW (Leibniz Information Centre for Economics) MediaTalk: Students in economics and business studies today draw on a wide range of information environments when searching for academic literature. Google Scholar, library catalogues and generative AI are part of their everyday research routines. But what role do traditional subject-specific databases still play? And how well do students manage to find information, assess its quality and use it correctly in an academic context? These questions are at the heart of our new study (in German) „Zwischen Google Scholar und ChatGPT – Wie Wirtschaftsstudierende heute recherchieren“ (“Between Google Scholar and ChatGPT – How economics and business students conduct research today”). Between March and May 2026, we conducted an online survey of 908 economics and business students at German universities. Research habits are shifting The results show, first of all, that independent literature searching is routine for the vast majority of the surveyed students: 88.3 per cent have searched for literature or specialist information on their own, either frequently or occasionally. General search engines remain the most widely used tools, with 91.3 per cent of those with research experience using Google, Google Scholar or similar services sometimes or often. US colleges and universities are grappling with federal and state disinvestment and intervention at a time when AI and other technologies are reshaping how research is conducted and its findings are communicated. As a result, researchers at US higher education institutions are operating in an unstable environment. Against this backdrop, the findings from our survey of 4,003 researchers, fielded in late 2025, demonstrate that they remain committed to carrying out essential work and that they are doing so in innovative ways—through collaboration, the creation of valuable educational experiences, and pushing knowledge towards the next frontier. items.raw_text: Acknowledgments: The author thanks Hayley Park of the University of Maryland for her contributions to language used in this article and Derek Wilmott of the University of Toledo for his assistance in developing the incident reporting form. Libraries across the country are navigating heightened immigration enforcement activity while trying to support community members and staff. Library leaders may face difficult decisions about how to respond to enforcement activity, address harassment, communicate with their communities, and protect patrons and employees, often with limited information about what other libraries are experiencing. Consider a public library responding to increased immigration enforcement activity in its community. Library leadership might consider issuing a public statement supporting immigrants but ultimately decide against it after consulting legal counsel, concerned that doing so could make the library a target. How can library leaders make decisions like this when much of the information available to them comes from anecdotal experiences or informal conversations with colleagues? Better data can help. items.title: Art for Everyone: How Public Libraries Expand Access
items.raw_text: Introducing children to viewing, creating, and enjoying art at a young age helps them appreciate it throughout their lives. Some children are exposed to various forms of art because it is part of their daily life or because they have easy access to museums and galleries in their community. But in many areas across the country, access to museums and art galleries can be cost prohibitive. That is where the public library comes in! While some museums, including the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., offer free admission, millions of people across the country do not have easy access to them. According to the 2024 Annual Survey of Museum-Goers from the American Alliance of Museums and Wilkening Consulting, museum admission costs vary widely, from a few dollars to $40–$50 per adult at some institutions. Among U.S. adults who visit museums at least occasionally, cost was the number one barrier to visiting more often. Among frequent museum-goers, younger adults were twice as likely as seniors to be concerned about admission costs. In response to those barriers, and in an effort to enrich and inspire customers of all ages, many library systems have stepped up to provide access to art in a variety of forms. items.title: Autism Acceptance at All Ages
items.raw_text: Autism acceptance efforts have come a long way in recent years, and libraries are one of the key reasons why. As a librarian and the mother of two sons with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), I’ve witnessed this progress firsthand. Through our “See Beyond the Spectrum” initiative, in recent years, BML has established new ASD-friendly programs, made our existing programs more accessible, updated our collections with texts by autistic writers, and established an autism caregiver support group. Our staff have gone through autism awareness training, and we’ve established partnerships with local organizations that serve autistic youth. Much of this workhas been supported by external grants, including generous funding from the ALA’s “Libraries Transforming Communities” initiative, which seeks to help libraries become more accessible to patrons with disabilities. Everything we’ve done has proved beneficial, both inside and outside of the library. Staff-patron interactions are more productive and less awkward. items.title: The Librarian’s New Role: Knowledge Discovery
items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. It represents a fundamental change in the relationship between people and information. The question librarians should be asking is not whether artificial intelligence can answer questions. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. items.title: Expanding Access Through Inclusive Collections
items.raw_text: Receiving a scholarship to attend PLA 2026 in Minneapolis gave me the opportunity to learn from innovative libraries and inspiring information professionals. One session in particular, “Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities,” presented by Plano Public Library and Libraries for All LLC, reinforced a simple but urgent idea: if members of our community cannot meaningfully use our materials, we are not fully meeting our mission. Access is about more than having a collection. It is about ensuring that everyone can engage with and benefit from it. The session highlighted how people with disabilities are often underserved by traditional library collections. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Some readers may have physical disabilities that make turning pages difficult. Others may benefit from visual supports, tactile elements, or alternative ways of interacting with a text. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. Before attending the session, my understanding of accessibility largely centered on traditional formats such as large print and braille. Learning about adaptive books expanded that perspective. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books.
